title: FHENDI: A Near-DRAM Accelerator for Compiler-Generated Fully Homomorphic Encryption Applications
problem: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) workloads are both compute- and memory-intensive, and even dedicated FHE ASICs are bottlenecked by expensive memory transfers due to large ciphertext operands and limited bank-to-bank communication, die-to-die bandwidth, and memory access latency within near-DRAM processing.
motivation: FHE enables privacy-preserving cloud computation on encrypted data, but the extreme memory bandwidth requirements of NTT, polynomial multiplication, and bootstrapping make purely compute-centric acceleration insufficient.
method: FHENDI is a hierarchical near-DRAM processing (NDP) architecture that exploits four levels of FHE parallelism (element-wise, limb-wise, coefficient-wise, ciphertext-wise) mapped to different hierarchy levels. Bank-to-bank communication is addressed via a conflict-free mapping algorithm using localized permutation networks that enable element-wise and butterfly operations within DRAM subarrays. Die-to-die bandwidth constraints are addressed by pipelining parallel bootstrapping operations identified by the HElayers compiler. Memory access latency is hidden using a dual-banking scheme combined with subarray-level parallelism (SLP). The system is evaluated with compiled FHE programs for CNN/Transformer ML inference, database range query, and sorting.
key_novelty: A conflict-free localized permutation network enabling efficient bank-local element-wise and butterfly NTT operations in near-DRAM, eliminating the need for inter-bank communication in FHE.
contributions: FHENDI hierarchical NDP design exploiting four parallelism levels in FHE workloads
Conflict-free bank-local permutation network for element-wise and butterfly operations
Pipelined bootstrapping to address die-to-die bandwidth limits using HElayers compiler output
Mean speedups of 2145.8x over server CPU, 118.29x over GPU, 2.45x over FHE ASIC

metrics.speedup: 2145.8x vs server CPU, 118.29x vs GPU, 2.45x vs FHE ASIC (mean across workloads)

limitations: Not discussed; the 2.45x gain over FHE ASIC suggests the baseline ASIC is more memory-optimized, and the margin may narrow with future DRAM technology improvements.
primary_theme: near-DRAM acceleration for fully homomorphic encryption
